q: The wavelength of a violet laser diode is $405\,\text{nm}$. Estimate its threshold voltage.
a: At the threshold voltage $eU_\text{k} \approx \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, so $U_\text{k} \approx \tfrac{hc}{e\lambda}$. First we calculate $hc = 1.9865 \cdot 10^{-25}\,\text{J}\,\text{m}$ and $e\lambda = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C} \cdot 405 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m} = 6.488 \cdot 10^{-26}\,\text{C}\,\text{m}$, so $U_\text{k} \approx 1.9865 \cdot 10^{-25}\,\text{J}\,\text{m} : 6.488 \cdot 10^{-26}\,\text{C}\,\text{m} = 3.06\,\text{V}$. Each electron must receive from the voltage source approximately the energy of one photon, $3.06\,\text{eV}$; the measured threshold voltage is usually slightly smaller than this.

q: The wavelength of the light source is needed in measuring the Planck constant. Why is the wavelength of a laser diode known more accurately than that of an LED?
a: The spectrum of a laser diode is a very narrow line, about $1\,\text{nm}$ wide, so its wavelength is almost unambiguous. The spectrum of an LED is a band $20$–$40\,\text{nm}$ wide, so the wavelength of the peak given as its wavelength is less accurate, and the uncertainty is transferred to the frequency $f = \tfrac{c}{\lambda}$.
